🗺️The level problem, and the rule that fixes it

You wrote“You already list AIMCo and BCI, which are investment managers, not single pension plans… otherwise you end up with the allocator equivalent of putting ‘Europe’ and ‘France’ in the same column.”
The rule this sheet now follows

A row earns a place in Section A if it can sign a subscription agreement for a fund it chose. Everything else is context. The Level column says which kind of thing each row is, and the “Decision sits with” column names the building to call.

The four managers below run money for eight of the plans on your list. That is the whole of your points 5, 6, 9 and 10. AIMCo’s own client list adds three more that were not on your list either: the Alberta Teachers’ Retirement Fund at C$26.7bn, Management Employees at C$7.8bn and Universities Academic at C$2.6bn. All three are on the sheet as context.

The lock-in is statutory, not a habit. Alberta’s audited statements say pool participants “have no control over the management of the pool and the selection of securities in the pool.” BCI’s governance materials put investment authority with its CEO and CIO under the Public Sector Pension Plans Act and say its own board is precluded from involvement. A plan in Section B cannot be argued into a commitment.

🔎Three findings that change the call list

Suncor is the buried lead

Its 40-F restricts plan assets to “pooled, mutual, segregated or exchange traded funds”, and the private debt and equity sleeve went from 2% to 8% of C$7.76bn in a single year. No in-house private equity team, contractually confined to commingled vehicles, deploying now. That is the fund-of-funds buyer profile written out. The blocker is finding the person, not the fit.

Air Canada’s money is a real asset manager

Trans-Canada Capital runs the plans and third-party capital, and operates a C$9.0bn evergreen private-markets fund holding private equity and co-investments. Vincent Morin is President and CIO. The Pionairs hold no assets and are not investors.

Alberta is retrenching from Asia

AIMCo closed its Singapore and New York offices in February 2025, about 17 months after opening Singapore, and the head of Singapore left. Its 2025 Asia-Pacific activity is infrastructure, not private equity. A Singapore-based Asia fund-of-funds is walking into a retreat, not a gap. BCI is a harder version of the same problem: Asia is already 11.5% of its private equity book, directs are about 45% of it, and it sold C$1.6bn to C$1.9bn of secondaries in FY2025 to cut intermediated exposure.

Pavilion wins. HarbourVest has had no Asia-dedicated commingled fund in market since December 2022. An LP that bought HIPEP V-Asia Pacific, HIPEP VI-Asia Pacific or HIPEP VII Asia Pacific approved an Asia fund-of-funds and now has no HarbourVest product to re-up into except a combined Europe and Asia fund. Pavilion sells the thing that slot was built for, with a written Japan 30 / China 20 / Korea 20 / India-SEA-ANZ 30 split where HIPEP X gives no Asia weight at all. HarbourVest publishes no China-excluded option, so an LP with a China restriction has to negotiate a side letter or buy Pavilion's exclusion sleeve off the shelf. On price, 1 per cent and 10 per cent blended undercuts a conventional fund-of-funds load, and Pavilion is resident in Asia with a Singapore parent rather than running the region from Boston.
Pavilion loses. HarbourVest has been in Asia for over 25 years, has six offices in the region, 233 investment professionals and USD 161bn of assets, and has committed more than USD 29bn across Europe and Asia. Pavilion is a first-time fund with a first close eight quarters out. On most investment committees that comparison ends the meeting, and a Temasek parent does not fix it. HarbourVest is also already on the roster at many of the institutions Pavilion wants: Pennsylvania SERS, CalSTRS, Virginia Retirement System, AP7, BCI, NEST, Norfolk, Shropshire, Lewisham, Tyne and Wear, West Midlands and West Yorkshire all hold a HarbourVest vehicle or mandate. A CIO who wants more Asia can ask the incumbent to build an Asia sleeve inside an existing separate account, which costs one email and no new manager approval. HarbourVest demonstrably does this already, through HIPEP Select Asia I to III and the VSMA1 Asia separate account. The four-year gap cuts both ways: HarbourVest may have stopped selling the commingled Asia fund because Western LPs stopped buying Asia, in which case the orphaned slot Pavilion is aiming at may have been closed deliberately rather than left open.

Partners Group also opened a seventh Asian office in 2024, so it can tell the same client that Asia is covered inside a global mandate, from a 1996 firm with USD 186bn of AUM, more than 800 institutional clients and a SIX listing since 2006. Pavilion arrives with fund one and a first close still ahead of it in 4Q 2026.

A trustee who lived through that will ask why a first-time Seviora vehicle raising US$1.5bn with a US$50m preferred ticket ends differently, and Pavilion has no fund track record of its own to answer with. Pavilion's Temasek parent helps here, because a state-owned Singapore holding company is a more durable sponsor than a Hong Kong family office or a listed UK asset manager, and Jodi should lead with that rather than with performance. The counter she will hear is that Asia fund-of-funds fees were the reason these programmes were cut, and 1 percent and 10 percent blended is still a fee layer on top of the underlying GPs.

LTD., UEN 201536711Z, a live Singapore consultancy incorporated 2015-10-05, but Emerald Hill is a Singapore street name and nothing links that company to this manager, so it is recorded here as a non-match.
Ownership and background
Independent. F: the Fund III Form D names Sangyun Choung and Michael Smith as directors and the Fund II Form D names S. Choung, David Spencer and Michael Smith as executive officers. No parent, bank owner or insurer owner appears in any filing. F: the Fund II Form D was filed from a Denver, Colorado address and the Fund III filing lists related persons in Lakewood, Colorado and London, so the firm ran a US arm alongside Hong Kong.
Overlap with Pavilion: full
🟢
LPs unserved
Emerald Hill Capital Partners III, L.P., final close US$400m in May 2014. F: no Fund IV exists on any record I could reach. EDGAR full-text search across every form type returns exactly five filings naming the firm, all Form D or Form D amendments, and the last is dated 2013-06-10. F: a Fund I is implied by the second and third fund labels used in the 2010 and 2014 trade press, but no source I opened names it, so it is omitted from the fund list rather than guessed at.
Asia-wide, with no published country split. F: China Money Network and AltAssets both describe the vehicles as Asian fund-of-funds, and the surviving website tagline reads Passionately Dedicated to Helping our Clients Build Successful Private Equity Portfolios in Asia. I: no evidence suggests this was a China book wearing an Asia label, but no percentage allocation was ever disclosed, so Jodi cannot set Pavilion's Japan 30 / China 20 / Korea 20 split against a published comparator here.
China: Not found. The firm stopped raising before the ex-China sleeve became a standard ask, and no public statement on China weighting or exclusion exists. · ex-China option not found
No named investor found on the public record.
Pavilion wins. Emerald Hill closed a US$400m Asia fund-of-funds in May 2014 and its Hong Kong licence ended on 12 May 2016. Thirty-one investor slots across Fund III and Fund III-A, and thirteen more in Fund II, have had no successor vehicle for over a decade. Those LPs are documented as endowments, foundations, pensions, insurers and family offices, and every one of them has already cleared a fund-of-funds structure, an Asia blind pool and a non-domestic boutique manager. Pavilion answers the failure mode directly. A Temasek-owned parent and a US$1.5bn target say the manager will still be there for Fund II, and 1% with 10% carry blended is a defensible price for a rebuilt relationship.
Pavilion loses. Emerald Hill raised US$300m and US$400m, so an investor that chose it was buying a small and selective book, and Pavilion at US$1.5bn with a US$50m preferred ticket is a different product entirely. A family office or foundation that wrote US$10m into Fund III cannot clear a US$50m minimum, which removes a large part of this orphaned list on arithmetic alone. The manager also vanished, so some of these LPs concluded that Asia fund-of-funds is a structure that fails rather than a manager that failed, and Pavilion has no performance record on this platform to argue otherwise. Temasek ownership helps on survival and hurts with any investor that wants a manager with no state shareholder sitting behind it.
Axiom Asia Private Capital
Singapore · founded 2006
Ownership and background
Independent and partner-owned. No bank, insurer or listed parent found. Edmond Ng and Marc Lau founded the firm in 2006, Chris Loh and Alex Lee joined in 2009, and all four are managing partners. Ng, Loh and Lau came from GIC Special Investments, so the house has a Singapore sovereign-fund lineage of its own. Two co-founders exited before Fund IV. The firm is registered with the SEC as Axiom Asia Private Capital Management Services, LP, CRD 163156.
Overlap with Pavilion: full
🟡
Between funds
Axiom Asia 7, L.P., final close US$1.28bn on 27 March 2025 against the US$1.8bn total offering recorded on its Form D. The vehicle actually selling today is Axiom Asia Opportunity Fund 2, US$63m sold from five investors as at the 1 April 2026 Form D.
Fund VII holds China at 5 to 15 percent. Australia, Japan and South Korea are each expected at 15 to 25 percent. India rises to roughly the same weight as China. Southeast Asia is taken opportunistically with no published percentage. Against Pavilion's Japan 30 / China 20 / Korea 20 / India-SEA-ANZ 30, Axiom is lighter on China and heavier on Australia.
China: Cutting China hard. China used to account for as much as half of the early Axiom fund-of-funds and sits at 5 to 15 percent in Fund VII. The managing partner told ION Analytics that 'the demand for foreign capital by Chinese businesses has dropped substantially' and that 'going forward, it's not going to be easy to put money to work in China at the same level as they have in the past'. The firm is moving the book toward developed Asia. · ex-China option not found

Pavilion wins. Axiom 7 closed at US$1.28bn against a US$1.8bn Form D offering and came in US$502m under Fund VI, so the incumbent's own LP base shrank and several approved Asia fund-of-funds slots are sitting unfilled. AP3 and the State of Michigan Retirement Systems each hold four to six older Axiom vehicles and neither shows Fund 7 on its latest holdings schedule, which is exactly the warm door Pavilion wants. Axiom has taken China down to 5 to 15 percent, so a buyer who still wants a deliberate 20 percent China weight has nowhere to put it inside Axiom, while Pavilion's China-exclusion sleeve serves the buyer on the other side of that question in the same fund. Pavilion's blended 1 percent and 10 percent, with zero fee and zero carry on the primary sleeve, is a hard number to argue against when Axiom publishes no terms at all. Axiom sells one commingled fund and declines separate accounts, so a US$50m-plus buyer who wants a tailored mandate has to look past it, and Pavilion's co-invest sleeve moving from 40 to 50 percent gives that buyer the fee break Axiom's sidecar structure does not.
Pavilion loses. Axiom is on its seventh flagship with a twenty-year record, six prior vintages of realised performance and a named institutional list that includes Montana, the State of Michigan, STRS Ohio, MOSERS, AP3, West Midlands and Caledonia. Pavilion Fund I has none of that, and a first-time vehicle with a 4Q 2026 first close fails most consultant screens on track record before anyone reads the terms. Axiom's founders came out of GIC Special Investments and the firm is partner-owned, which lets Axiom argue that Pavilion's Temasek parent creates a conflict on Singapore and Southeast Asia deals and a political overlay on every allocation decision, and that argument lands hardest with the US public plans that are the deepest part of Axiom's book. Because Axiom publishes no fee terms, Pavilion's 1 and 10 has no public number to beat and the pricing case has to be made blind in the room. An existing Axiom LP re-ups with no new operational due diligence, no new legal spend and no new committee paper, so Pavilion's 12+1+1 term, 8 percent preferred return and US$50m preferred ticket have to overcome a switching cost the incumbent never pays. Axiom's retreat from China to 5 to 15 percent also matches where most 2026 allocators already want to be, so Pavilion's 20 percent China weight reads as risk rather than differentiation to a large part of the buyer set.
Asia Alternatives Management LLC
San Francisco, California (SEC principal office, One Embarcadero Center, 16th Floor). New Jersey's 2016 board memo records the firm's headquarters as Hong Kong, so the firm presents Hong Kong as its Asia base. · founded 2005
Ownership and background
Independent and partner-owned. Founded in 2005 by Melissa Ma, Laure Wang and Rebecca Xu. No outside stake in the management company was found on the public record, and the 2026-07-29 Form ADV shows no parent. The firm itself holds a minority stake in a separate entity, Franklin Templeton Private Equity LLC, a joint venture announced on 10 September 2018 in which Franklin Templeton is the majority owner and Asia Alternatives and the FTPE management team hold minority stakes. The New Jersey 2020 memo records the year founded as 2006, which conflicts with the 2005 date in the firm's own 2015 and 2017 releases.
Overlap with Pavilion: full
🔴
In market
Asia Alternatives Capital Partners VII, LP. Form D filed 2025-10-27 with five parallel vehicles, indefinite offering amount and zero sold at filing. Mergermarket reported a US$900m first close in 4Q25 against a US$800m target for the flagship commingled fund and a US$1.4bn overall target including separate accounts. No press release for Fund VII appears on the firm's own site, where the most recent item is the January 2022 Fund VI close.
Greater China (Mainland China, Taiwan and Hong Kong), Japan, Korea, South East Asia, India and Australia. No published percentage split was found. The firm said in its January 2022 release that China continues to be its largest single country exposure, and that its Japan buyout partnerships have become significant sources of performance in recent years. The co-investment series count tells the same story: China Growth runs to XV and China Venture to N, against Japan Buyout VII and Korea Buyout VI. This is a genuine pan-Asia platform with a China-weighted book, not a China fund wearing an Asia label, but the China weight is the live objection.
Terms: fee Separate-account terms are public in two New Jersey board memos. The 2016 New Jersey Asia Investors III account charged 0.8% of capital commitments on the balanced pool, reduced to 0.5% of invested amount on the earlier of a successor fund or the end of the investment period, no fee on the co-investment pool, blended to an average 0.2% a year. The 2020 New Jersey separate account charged 0.80% stepping to 0.50% on the pro-rata pool, no fee on the overage pool, blended 0.40% stepping to 0.25%. Commingled AACP fund terms were not found on the public record. · carry 2016 New Jersey account: 6.075% on the balanced pool, none on the co-investment pool, blended 3.0375%, with a 100% fee offset. 2020 New Jersey account: 5.85% profit allocation on the pro-rata pool, none on the overage pool, blended 2.925%. · hurdle 8.0% hurdle on the balanced pool in the 2016 account and 8% in the 2020 account.
China: Both doors are open. China is still the largest single country exposure and the China co-investment programme is live, with AACP China Growth Investors XV filing a Form D on 2026-05-14. At the same time the firm now sells a formal ex-China route: it filed Form D on 2025-10-27 for Asia Alternatives Capital Partners VII (Ex-China), LP and AACP Tax-Exempt Investors VII (Ex-China), L.P. as parallel vehicles to the main Fund VII. Carve-out sleeves are an old habit here, since AACP IV Ex-Japan Investors, LP dates from 2014. Mergermarket reported in July 2025 that the firm was selling more than US$800m of fund positions from the earlier vehicles, a portfolio of over 20 China, India, Japan and pan-Asia positions, through Jefferies. · ex-China option yes

Pavilion wins. Asia Alternatives runs a China-weighted book. It told the market in January 2022 that China remains its largest single country exposure, and its co-investment series has reached AACP China Growth Investors XV while Japan Buyout stops at VII. Pavilion sells Japan 30 and China 20, which is the shape most 2026 investment committees are actually asking for. Pavilion's Temasek parent is an asset in Asia itself, because it buys Singapore and regional general partner access that a San Francisco adviser has to earn with travel. The competitor is also shrinking. Regulatory AUM fell from about US$16.5bn to US$13.24bn, it sold more than US$800m of fund positions through Jefferies in 2025, and it has published nothing at all about Fund VII. An LP who wants a manager with room to grow has a reason to hear Pavilion out. Pavilion's co-investment weighting of 40 moving to 50 is also higher than the pro-rata pools Asia Alternatives writes into its separate accounts.
Pavilion loses. Pavilion loses this one on price and on record. New Jersey's own board papers put the Asia Alternatives separate account at a blended 0.40% management fee stepping to 0.25%, a blended 2.925% profit allocation and an 8% hurdle, with no fee and no carry at all on the overage pool. The 2016 account was cheaper still at a blended 0.2% and 3.04%. Pavilion asks 1% and 10% blended on the same 8% preferred return. A US$50m ticket buyer puts those two numbers side by side and Pavilion is several times the fee and three times the carry, and the buyer will say so out loud. Record is the second problem. Asia Alternatives is on its seventh flagship with a first vintage of 2007, and Pennsylvania SERS has funded six separate Asia Alternatives vehicles since June 2007 and still holds them. Pavilion Fund I has no realised Asia fund-of-funds track record of its own and a first close that has not happened yet. Temasek ownership cuts against Pavilion here. A US state fund that is already trimming China will ask harder questions of a Singapore sovereign wealth subsidiary than of a partner-owned US registered adviser, and Asia Alternatives is the one with the clean answer on that point.

Temasek ownership cuts against Pavilion with Australian super funds, which run their own state-ownership and China-exposure screens and already have a local Asia-Pacific manager on the panel.

Pavilion wins. Size and structure. Adams Street Asia Fund II has sold USD 90.1m to four investors after two years in market, and its predecessor raised USD 100.4m from six. A USD 50m ticket would make an LP a dominant holder of a sub-scale fund, and a large institution that wants a USD 1.5bn pan-Asia vehicle with a named co-investment and direct-secondaries programme cannot get it here. Adams Street also excludes China from its Asia primary practice by construction, so an LP that wants the full pan-Asia opportunity including China has to go elsewhere; Pavilion offers both, with China in the flagship and out of the sleeve. Adams Street's Asia funds are primaries-led with no Asia secondaries vehicle, which leaves Pavilion's direct-secondaries sleeve uncontested at this manager.
Pavilion loses. The brief's hypothesis was that Adams Street sells no Asia-dedicated product. That is wrong, and the correction is the finding. Adams Street Asia Fund II LP is raising right now, and its Asia primary practice is described by the firm as covering 'Asian investments ex-China, specifically in India, Australia, Japan, Southeast Asia, and Korea'. That is Pavilion's China-exclusion sleeve, already built, already funded, from a 1972 firm with USD 76bn, employee ownership, six Asia-Pacific offices, a Singapore-based partner who has led Asia primaries for years, and an Asia research programme running since 1999. An LP choosing between an ex-China Asia fund from Adams Street and one from a first-time Temasek-owned vehicle closing in 4Q 2026 has an easy answer on track record and on domicile. Every UK and Canadian institution evidenced above already holds Adams Street globally, so the incumbency is in place too. Pavilion's counter is scale and breadth, not credibility.

Ownership has changed and the widely repeated "majority owned by Tikehau Capital" line is out of date. Tikehau Capital announced a majority equity stake on 6 July 2021. Ltd., 1 Wallich Street #15-03 Guoco Tower, Singapore 078881, which appears as a fully consolidated Tikehau subsidiary at 100.0% of interest at both 31 December 2022 and 31 December 2023 in the Tikehau Capital 2023 Universal Registration Document, with the note "Tikehau Capital acquired 50.1% of the shares as part of the acquisition completed in 2021, and has an option to acquire the remaining 49.9% within two years of the acquisition date". Tikehau then sold it. The Tikehau Capital 2024 Universal Registration Document states under changes in the scope of consolidation: "The subsidiary FPE Investment Advisors (Singapore) was sold in April 2024 for an amount of US$3 million. FPE Investment Advisors is a founder-operated private equity player that specialises in delivering innovative secondary solutions to general partners (GPs) and Limited Partners (LPs) across Asia. The company is no longer consolidated as from April 2024 and the impacts of this operation are not material in the Group’s consolidated financial statements." A second note in the same document reads "The subsidiary FPE Investment Advisors was sold during the first half of 2024", and the cash-flow note records the disposal at EUR 0.9 million of cash. The Tikehau Capital 2025 Universal Registration Document contains no mention of Foundation at all. The buyer is not named in any Tikehau document. The US$3 million price and the description "founder-operated" point to a management buyback, and that is inference, not fact. Foundation PE’s own website still carries the July 2021 partnership announcement and says nothing about the 2024 sale. Founded in 2017 by Jason Sambanju, previously co-head of Asia at Paul Capital and head of Asian private equity secondaries at Deutsche Bank, with co-founder Jeremy Foo.

Any Hong Kong, Taiwanese, Korean, Malaysian or UK investor in Altrium III can ask why Seviora needs two multi-manager private-equity products and which one the group will feed. Temasek ownership cuts against Pavilion in that conversation, because it turns a differentiator into an internal channel conflict over one shared buyer list. The unnamed roster is the practical problem for Jodi. Azalea publishes no investor names at all, so this competitor yields a map of buyer types and countries and not a prospect list.

Melissa asked“Any other L and XL LPs that you can add to the bubble chart as this would be the top priority LPs that we want to know.”
25 institutions, and the chart changes shape when you add them.
Your slide-5 directory holds 99 names: 83 of them sit in the S bucket, 9 reach L and none reaches XL. The chart therefore shows a market of small accounts, which is not the market. These 25 names sit at L and XL by the deck’s own definitions, and the column each one falls into is the route in.

The horizontal axis is the route in, which is the answer to question two applied name by name, ordered by how much the institution has already approved. Orphaned re-up held an Asia fund-of-funds and has no live manager behind the position. Add-on holds a live Asia fund-of-funds manager, whether or not it is one of the two Melissa named. Open door has no Asia fund-of-funds relationship of any kind on the record. Displacement holds both Asia Alternatives and Axiom Asia. The vertical axis is the typical single-fund ticket on a logarithmic scale.

🚪Add on, or displace

Melissa asked“What L and XL LPs are looking for in a new Asia manager, and what we must address. Would we position as a new Asia fund to add on or to displace existing Asia Alt / Axiom? Which is an easier journey? Are there L and XL LPs that have not committed to Asia Alt or Axiom and should we target them first?”
Add on, and work the seven who already own the format.
Ranked by what the institution has already approved rather than by how many names sit in each pile, add-on is the shorter journey and it has seven names. The orphaned re-up is shorter still and has two, one documented and one that needs confirming before the call.

First: the add-on. Seven names, and the argument is the geography mix.

Seven of the twenty-five hold a live Asia fund-of-funds manager. Five hold Asia Alternatives or Axiom Asia; two hold someone else, which is the same conversation with a different incumbent named. The format is already approved in every one of them, the committee has already taken the blind-pool question and the non-domestic-manager question, so the only thing left to sell is the difference in the book. Pavilion carries Japan at 20 percent and Korea at 20 percent against a 30 percent China line. Sell the difference in the mix, never the difference in the manager.

Second: the orphaned re-up. Two names here, twenty-one in the market.

An institution whose Asia fund-of-funds manager has left owes nobody a re-up and has approved everything that matters. Two of the twenty-five sit here. Northern LGPS is the documented one: its partner funds' legacy pan-Asia fund-of-funds have run down to residual values with no replacement, which is a fifteen-year vacancy on the diversified Asia line. Teacher Retirement System of Texas is the second, and the record behind it is a trade-press report of a US$100m Squadron commitment that should be checked against the plan's own commitment schedule before the call. Across the one hundred and eighty-two institutions in the cross-reference there are twenty-one. That pool is worth the confirming work.

Third: the open door. Thirteen names, the largest group and the slowest.

These thirteen have Asia private equity exposure and no Asia fund-of-funds relationship of any kind on the record. That is not a gap waiting to be filled. It means the format itself has to be sold before Pavilion can be, and several of them buy Asia direct or through single manager funds at nine figures. For those the product that converts is a separate account or a co-investment sleeve rather than Fund I. Work them, but do not build the quarter on them.

Last: displacement. Three names, and only if the LP opens it.

A switch needs an incumbent to underperform, a consultant to bless the change and a re-up year to land in. It puts a first-time third-party raise into a comparison against a manager with four vintages of audited numbers at the same LP. Take a displacement when the LP raises it. Do not open with one.

Across 182 named institutions in the cross-reference, 21 hold an Asia fund-of-funds position and have no live Asia fund-of-funds relationship left at all.

The correction worth making out loud. Melissa asked whether the LPs holding neither Asia Alternatives nor Axiom Asia should be targeted first. The split below answers that as asked: 17 of the 25 hold neither. That group is three different sales, and the route column separates them. Thirteen hold no Asia fund-of-funds of any kind, so the format has to be sold before Pavilion can be. Two hold a live Asia fund-of-funds run by someone other than the two named managers, which is an add-on with a different incumbent. Two held one whose manager has left the market, which is the warmest start on the list: Northern LGPS, whose legacy Asia funds have run down with no replacement, and Teacher Retirement System of Texas, whose commitment still needs confirming.

The strongest case against this position

The orphan pool is smaller and softer than a first pass suggests.

Counting any departed manager as an orphan produced a much larger number. It does not survive checking the vehicle behind each relationship: CalSTRS and Northern LGPS hold HarbourVest through US lower-middle-market and co-investment funds, not Asia funds. Northern LGPS is an orphan on its partner funds' Pantheon, Partners Group and Aberdeen positions rather than on that HarbourVest line, and CalSTRS was never an Asia orphan at all. Of the twenty-one that remain, the ones left holding only HarbourVest or Schroders have a warm answer available from the incumbent, because both still offer Asia inside a combined fund. The orphan list says which those are.

Ranking by journey puts the smallest pile first.

Add-on is seven of twenty-five and the orphan route is two. A pipeline built this way is a short pipeline. The ranking is about the order of work inside a quarter, not about where the eventual money comes from, and the open-door thirteen will produce more commitments in absolute terms if enough of them can be moved at all.

Almost nobody in the record holds two Asia fund-of-funds managers at once.

Three of the twenty-five hold both Asia Alternatives and Axiom Asia, and five hold one. If the market treats these managers as substitutes rather than complements, the add-on route is thinner than it looks and more of the universe is a displacement after all.

The biggest names are the least likely fund-of-funds buyers.

Several of the largest additions build Asia in house. Keva has bought a dedicated Asia separate account twice and a blind pool never. Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Ontario Teachers are large enough that Fund I is the wrong product to show them first.

What an L or XL investor needs addressed

What they screenWhere Pavilion stands todayWhat has to be in the data roomUrgency

A Western consultant asks this in meeting two.High
Key person after 31 March 2026The founding chief executive, whose Temasek chief-investment-officer history underwrites the track record, retired on 31 March 2026 per Seviora Group’s own release.Answer it before it is asked, with the fourteen-year continuity underneath the founder and a named key-person clause in the limited partnership agreement.High
Temasek ownership and alignmentState ownership cuts both ways. It is the alignment story and it is also the political screen at a US public plan.One sentence on the anchor commitment that Pavilion will stand behind in writing, plus the governance separation between Temasek as shareholder and Pavilion as fiduciary.High
China exposureThirty percent China against a US political climate in which Asia and China are read as the same word.Show the China sleeve as a sized, disclosed and adjustable line, and say whether an ex-China option exists. Several competitors sell one.High
Fee loadA fund-of-funds fee sits on top of underlying manager fees, and consultants model the total.Publish the all-in load with the co-investment layer netted in, because the co-investment is where the fee drag is recovered. Co-investment rightsThe co-investment engine is the part of this fund that survives Western diligence.Break the co-investment record out as its own series by vintage: net internal rate of return, multiple, distributions, deal count and the selection rate behind the flow ratio.Medium

The public roster gives that function a different owner than the deck does, and an allocator who checks will see it.Medium

🟢 What they will find attractive

Distributions in a market that has stopped receiving them

The scarce good in 2026 is realised cash, not marks. A 2012-vintage book with distributions to show is the opening line, not the track record page.

A vacancy, not a crowded field

Fourteen managers have left the Asia fund-of-funds market or put the line into run-off. Pavilion is selling into a gap rather than into a queue, and the gap is named and dated.

Co-investment flow that a fund commitment buys

Fund commitments buy information rights, and the co-investment flow is what those rights are worth. Put the actual ratio of co-investment offered to capital committed on the slide before the call. Without the figure this is the weakest of the six.

Genuine pan-Asia coverage

Japan and Korea at twenty percent each is a different book from the China-weighted incumbents, and it is the part of Asia that Western committees are currently willing to fund.

A balance-sheet investor beside the limited partners

Temasek ownership and a general-partner commitment mean the manager is in the fund, which is the alignment test every investment committee applies.

First-fund terms

Early investors can ask for the advisory-committee seat, the co-investment allocation and the fee step that a fourth-vintage manager will not give.

🔴 What they will not

First raise from a manager nobody in the West has underwritten

Never raised third-party capital means no reference limited partners, no prior fund documents and an operational due-diligence file that is being written for the first time.

Key person, and the timing of it

The founding chief executive retired six months ago. Every key-person screen finds it in one search.

State ownership

Temasek is the alignment story and the political story. Several US public plans will run a geopolitical screen before they run an investment one.

China at thirty percent

Read by a US committee as the headline, whatever the other seventy percent holds.

Fee on fee

A fund-of-funds pays twice, and a consultant models the total before the first meeting.

A first close that Europe cannot reach

A Q4 2026 first close is weeks away and no European institution underwrites a first-time Western raise, clears operational diligence and gets an investment-committee slot in that time. Say so first rather than being told.

What Jodi says on the call
  • Let me answer the question you actually asked, which is which journey is easier.
  • Add-on, and I would rank the list by what each institution has already signed off rather than by which of the two managers they hold.
  • Seven of the twenty-five already hold a live Asia fund-of-funds manager. Five of those hold Asia Alternatives or Axiom Asia and two hold someone else. In all seven the format is approved, so the only argument is the geography mix, and ours is genuinely different.
  • Your third idea was right that the ones holding neither are worth targeting, and I want to refine it rather than just agree. Seventeen hold neither, but thirteen of those hold no Asia fund-of-funds at all, which means we are selling the format before we sell ourselves. That is the biggest group and the slowest.
  • Two of the seventeen are warmer than the rest. An LP whose Asia fund-of-funds manager has left the market owes nobody a re-up. Northern LGPS is the clean one, with fifteen years of run-down Asia funds and no replacement. Texas Teachers is the second and I want to confirm its commitment before we use it. There are twenty-one across everything we cross-referenced.
  • Displacement is three names and I would take it only if the LP raises it first.
The slide changeNew slide 7, titled "Four routes in, ranked by what is already approved". Four columns, add-on then orphaned re-up then open door then displacement, each with the count of institutions behind it and the first move. Put the fourteen departed managers as a named strip along the bottom, because the names are the evidence.

🗓️Stratifying the S LPs, and when to call

Melissa asked“How to stratify and target the S LPs, and when to reach out”
83 small accounts are four jobs, not eighty relationships.
These institutions have already outsourced the decision. Outsourced investment office usage peaks exactly in this size band and falls to nothing at the top of the market, so the entity to cover is the gatekeeper, not the account. Stratify by who actually decides and the work collapses to four motions.
StratumCountWho actually decidesThe motionWhenEffort per dollar
Delegated foundations
Definition
US private, community, health-system and hospital foundations, all sub-USD 20m ticket.
Examples
McKnight Foundation; Cleveland Foundation; Denver Foundation; Polk Brothers Foundation; Hyams Foundation
42Increasingly not the foundation: 39% of private and 47% of community foundations now use an outsourced investment office and those that do outsource about 93% of assets; where there is no OCIO, the gate is the consultant's recommended list (FEG has 164 charitable clients, Prime Buchholz 206 with zero government clients) with the board investment committee ratifying.Do not run 42 separate relationships. Map each name to its OCIO or consultant first, then run one diligence process per gatekeeper: Callan's CallanDNA and Fiducient's and Prime Buchholz's databases are free and self-serve, Cambridge Associates and FEG are submit-and-wait inboxes. Pair that with a pooled route the small names can actually use - a Commonfund or FEG-style USD 1m-minimum sleeve, or an Asia feeder at USD 100k to 250k like the CAIS Access Fund Asia Fund IV precedent - because a USD 5m to 20m institutional minimum is 5 to 20% of a USD 100m foundation's entire corpus against an 8 to 11% total alternatives allocation.
www.commonfund.org www.callan.com www.cambridgeassociates.com
Approach the gatekeepers year-round since consultant research runs continuously; approach the foundations themselves May to June, when their audits sign off and their boards see final numbers, and again September to November. Avoid August.

High if covered one at a time, Low if covered through four to six gatekeepers

US college, university and museum endowments and their supporting foundations, all sub-USD 20m ticket.

Screen by average charitable-client size from Form ADV Item 5.D: SEI (USD 8.3m average, 465 charitable clients), Hirtle Callaghan (USD 12.5m, 123), TIFF (USD 49.8m, 37), Mercer (USD 60.5m, 1,034) and Commonfund OCIO (USD 69.2m, 124) are the firms whose books match these names, while GEM, Strategic Investment Group, Cambridge Associates OCIO and Investure (USD 348m to 960m average clients) are not. The slide changeNew slide 8, titled "The small accounts are four jobs, not eighty". Four rows, one per stratum, with the count from your own directory, who actually decides, and the one move that reaches the whole stratum. The point of the slide is that the gatekeeper count is small even though the account count is not.

The outreach calendar, by class

Every window below carries the fiscal year end or the published calendar that drives it. Lines marked inference are market practice rather than a document.

LP classMonthsWhat is openWhat to sendShut, and who decides
US public pensions
The year
A 30 June fiscal year: pacing plans and capital-market assumptions land January to March, private-equity annual program reviews March to June, and the live commitment votes cluster September to mid-December after June-30 performance is booked.
 January to March
Fact
 Next year's private-markets pacing is being written and the consultant's capital-market assumptions are voted (Oregon OPERF's PE Annual Review with Aksia and Pathway was the 4 March 2026 item; CalPERS Investment Committee sat 16-17 March).
www.oregon.gov
 One page on where an Asia fund-of-funds sits in the 2027 commitment budget, addressed to the private-markets director and the PE consultant, not the CIO. Mid-December to mid-January and the back half of August: CalPERS holds no board meetings in August, October or December, SWIB skips January and February, and the NJ State Investment Council has nothing between late October and late January.
Decides: Investment Committee or Private Markets Committee feeding the full board, but for a fund-of-funds ticket most plans decide at staff level under delegated authority (CalPERS: MID $1.25bn, Deputy CIO $2bn, CIO $3.0bn per fund; CalSTRS staff may commit up to 2% of PE NAV to a new commingled fund with no board vote; WSIB is the exception and votes every named fund in open session).
April to June
Fact
 The heaviest review window: the CalPERS Private Equity Annual Program Review is a June Investment Committee item (15 June 2026, Meketa attachment), and WSIB's Private Markets Committee voted named funds on 5 February and 2 April.
www.calpers.ca.gov
 Full DDQ and data room with track record, and a request for the on-site before the fiscal-year turn.
July to August
Fact
 Boards are on strategic-planning offsites (CalPERS 13-15 July, CalSTRS 21-23 July education-only, WSIB 14-16 July), so staff calendars are free while nothing can be voted.
www.calpers.ca.gov
 Staff-level introduction and a data-room invitation; never an approval ask.
September to October
Fact
 June-30 performance season plus live commitment votes: WSIB's Private Markets Committee voted GTCR XV and CD&R XIII on 3 September 2026 with the GPs presenting and the full board ratified 17 September; CalSTRS' Investment Committee sat 22-24 September with Meketa's PE report and the annual delegation review.
www.sib.wa.gov
 Final terms and a Q4 close timeline; at a board-vote plan this is the only slot that can still reach a Q4 2026 first close.
November to mid-December
Fact
 The last votes of the calendar year (CalPERS IC 16 November, CalSTRS 4-5 November, SWIB 15-16 December).
www.swib.state.wi.us
 Closing documents, or a reset of the ask into the next pacing cycle.
US endowments and foundations
The year
Endowments close 30 June and most private foundations close 31 December, boards meet roughly quarterly on calendars that skip August entirely, the annual policy-portfolio review clusters in late spring, and fiscal-year results publish September to February.
 September to early December
Fact
 Post-fiscal-close committee meetings (UTIMCO 24 September and 10 December 2026, Penn State 17-18 September and 12-13 November, UC Regents 20-22 September); NACUBO-Commonfund data collection runs September to December.
www.utimco.org
 The full Fund I pack with fiscal-year-dated performance and a pacing view for the new fiscal year. August above all - zero board or investment-committee meetings in August at UTIMCO, Penn State or the UC Regents - plus late June and July for the 30 June close and the start of audit fieldwork; note that July is not universally dead (UC Regents meet 20-21 July 2027, Penn State 22-23 July 2027).
Decides: Board or investment committee owns policy and asset allocation; manager and fund selection is delegated to the internal CIO, staff or an OCIO (the UC Investments Committee charter explicitly bars members from directing the selection of specific funds or managers).
October to November
Fact
 Audited statements land (Harvard's FY25 report published 16 October 2025, Notre Dame's PwC opinion dated 14 November 2025, UVIMCO's FY26 posted September 2026).
www.hmc.harvard.edu
 A note referencing their just-published numbers and a request for the Q4 or Q1 committee slot.
Mid-January to mid-March
Fact
 The peer-benchmark moment: NCSE FY25 results published 12 February 2026 and FY26 results are due February 2027; the Ford Foundation's annual trustee meeting is the second Thursday in February; UTIMCO sits 5 March.
www.nacubo.org
 A benchmark-relative pitch with a first-close date attached.
April to mid-June
Fact
 The annual asset-allocation review, where target weights actually change: UTIMCO's 18 June 2026 annual meeting ran the FY2027 Policy Review and amended asset-class targets and ranges effective 1 September 2026.
www.utimco.org
 New-sleeve or new-geography asks - an Asia PE line item, not a fund pitch.
May to June (foundations only)
Fact
 Private foundations run the inverted rhythm: audits sign off late May to June (Ford 18 June 2026, Kresge 5 June 2025, Hewlett 29 May 2026, RWJF 1 June 2026), so foundation boards see final numbers at a June or summer meeting when endowments are dark.
www.fordfoundation.org
 Foundation-specific outreach timed to the June board, while endowment coverage is paused.
Canadian plans
The year
Two clocks that never synchronise: five December-31 plans (OTPP, OMERS, HOOPP, CDPQ, IMCO) set next year's plan in November and December effective 1 January and publish results 20 February to 10 March, while four March-31 plans (CPP Investments, PSP, BCI, AIMCo) start a fresh budget year on 1 April and publish results 21 May to 26 June.
 Late September to mid-November
Fact
 The December-31 plans' investment committees are in their heaviest run and next year's operating plan is being drafted; OMERS' board approves the Consolidated Operating Plan and the Statements of Investment Policies and Procedures in December, effective 1 January.
www.omers.com
 The full fund pack, so it is underwritten into 2027 pacing rather than pitched against an already-set plan. Mid-February to mid-March (OMERS 23 February, CDPQ 24 February, IMCO 5 March, OTPP 6 March, HOOPP 10 March) and mid-May to late June (CPP Investments 21 May, PSP 16 June, BCI 25 June, AIMCo 26 June) are annual-report lockdown; late December is a write-off.
Decides: Management inside a board-approved framework - the board approves the framework and the annual plan, not the individual commitment; PSP is the exception, its board-level Investment and Risk Committee reviewed and approved new investment managers and investment opportunities in FY2026.
January to early February
Fact
 The December-31 plans open a new risk-budget year; OTPP states its board approves total-fund active risk allocations at the beginning of each year.
www.otpp.com
 A meeting request plus a one-page fit against the new year's PE pacing.
Late March to April
Fact
 The March-31 plans roll into a new fiscal year with a board-approved business plan in hand; CPP Investments' board approves the annual business plan and its Investment Strategy Committee approves the framework for engaging external managers.
www.investpsp.com
 The commitment ask itself.
July to October
Inference
 The only stretch with no results cycle and no plan-setting deadline on either clock; BCI's board meets quarterly plus extras and IMCO not less than once each quarter.
www.bci.ca
 Relationship meetings, on-sites and co-investment samples.
UK institutions (LGPS pools, USS, Railpen, corporate DB)
The year
A 31 March fiscal year in which January to March sets strategy and money for 1 April, spring opens the pools' private-markets vintage, and July to October is audit season - but 2026-27 is abnormal because manager selection has just moved by statute from the individual funds to the pools.
 September to December 2026
Fact
 Border to Coast states the seven Partner Funds that joined in 2026 will confirm their commitments later this year, and autumn committees sit (Cornwall 17 September, 29 October, 18 December 2026; LPFA Investment Committee 17 September and 7 December 2026).
www.bordertocoast.org.uk
 Material into the pool investment teams about three weeks before each date - this is the live window for a Q4 2026 close. Mid-July through August is audit and annual-report drafting (USS' accounts were signed 21 July 2026, Border to Coast publishes in July, and neither Cornwall nor LPFA has a July or August committee date in 2026), plus late March to mid-April for year-end close.
Decides: The administering authority's Pensions Committee sets strategy and SAA; the pool company decides manager selection - the 29 June 2026 statutory guidance states all investment management decisions below the investment strategy, including investment manager selection, must be made by the pool.
January to mid-March
Fact
 Strategic asset allocation sign-off and the next fiscal year's business plan; every England and Wales fund must publish a new Investment Strategy Statement on or before 31 March 2027 under SI 2026/544 regulation 13(2).
www.legislation.gov.uk
 An asset-class-level case sized to a single private-markets SAA line, addressed to the pool rather than a fund pitch to the council.
March to April
Fact
 The pool commitment vintage: Border to Coast launched Series 3A in April 2025 at GBP 2.4bn and nine Partner Funds committed a further GBP 2.4bn to Series 3B in March 2026, each with a one-year commitment period.
www.bordertocoast.org.uk
 Full fund terms, DDQ, capacity and close dates - this is where money actually moves.
Quarterly, year-round
Fact
 Pool-level shareholder touchpoints: London CIV holds two General Meetings and four Shareholder Committees a year, and the Wales Pension Partnership's Joint Governance Committee meets a minimum of four times a year.
londonciv.org.uk
 Pool-strategy positioning, since shareholder reserved matters include the business plan.
Nordic institutions (AP funds, Danish labour-market funds, Finnish pension companies)
The year
A 31 December fiscal year that reports in February, re-boards at the end of May, vanishes in July by statute, thinks strategically August to October, and locks budget and plan in November and December - so a Q4 2026 close must already be in staff hands rather than introduced now.
 August to October
Fact
 The strategy window: AP3 holds its annual strategy meeting in August and AP2's 2025 strategy meeting was in October covering the long-term business plan; AP2's board held six ordinary plus two extraordinary meetings, AP3 seven and AP4 eight.
a.storyblok.com
 The strategic case - why Asia PE and why a fund-of-funds; an argument not in staff hands before the strategy meeting cannot be board-ready in December. July is statutory and total in Sweden and Finland - Sweden's Semesterlag 1977:480 section 12 requires a leave period of at least four weeks during June to August and Finland requires a 24-day summer holiday inside 2 May to 30 September taken uninterrupted; secondary dead zone is early February to late March, the annual-reporting crunch (ATP signed 4 February 2026, Ilmarinen 13 February, AP2 16 February, AP4 19 February, AP3 25 February).
Decides: The Board of Directors, which annually adopts the business plan with the strategic asset allocation (AP2); ATP's Supervisory Board determines the frameworks for ATP's investments; Keva's Board decides the pension fund investment plan by law.
Late September to mid-November
Fact
 The AP2 and AP3 October boards take the quarterly report, budget monitoring and risk tolerance; KLP's published calendar puts Q3 on 12 November 2026.
ap2.se
 The full pack in ILPA DDQ format - AP2 asks PE managers to follow ILPA and UNPRI guidelines including the ILPA Due Diligence Information Request.
November to December
Fact
 Decision: AP2's board annually approves the budget, business plan and strategic asset allocation, AP4 booked a business plan for 2026 including budget, and AP3's December board takes budget.
ap2.se
 Final terms and the commitment paper; nothing new introduced here lands.
Mid-April to late May
Fact
 Preparatory: AP3's April quarterly board, and ATP's Supervisory Board convened ordinarily seven times in 2025.
www.atp.dk
 Introduction meetings, Asia fund-of-funds education and a DDQ pre-read; avoid the last week of May, when the Government appoints AP boards (AP2's board was decided 28 May 2025).
2026 calendar year (AP4 specifically)
Inference
 AP4 states that in 2026 it will carry out a new ALM analysis; its ALM runs every three years and the Dynamic Normal Portfolio is reviewed every two.
www.ap4.se
 A new-asset-class case timed into the ALM, the rare moment a new class can enter.
Continental European institutions (Dutch fiduciaries, German, French, Italian, insurers)
The year
A 31 December fiscal year with two decision seasons - spring reporting (Dutch jaarverslag late April, insurer results March, AGM April) and an autumn-to-early-winter commitment season (Italian casse SAA in October, German SAA and Verwaltungsrat in November, Dutch bestuur policy November to December) - broken by a hard August stop, with France uniquely setting its strategic allocation in June.
 Late September to October
Fact
 The best single window for a Q4 close: Italian casse delegate assemblies set multi-year SAA (Inarcassa's Comitato Nazionale dei Delegati approved the Asset Allocation Strategica 2026-2030 at its 16-17 October 2025 meeting) and Dutch investment committees run pre-decision agendas (ABP's commissie beleggingen met nine times in 2024).
www.inarcassa.it
 Full data room and the SAA-fit case. August in all three markets, with statute behind it: 15 August is a jour ferie under French Code du travail L3133-1 and a giorno festivo under Italian Legge 260/1949, Germany's BUrlG sections 3 and 7(2) require a contiguous block of at least 12 working days and the KMK Ferienkalender puts every Land out simultaneously in the first week of August; secondary dead zone is roughly 20 December to 6 January.
Decides: Netherlands: het bestuur adopts the strategic investment plan and SAA, prepared by the commissie beleggingen on an ALM foundation. France: FRR's Conseil de surveillance adopts the allocation annually. Italy: the Consiglio di Amministrazione approves investments (Enpam) and the Comitato Nazionale dei Delegati approves the SAA (Inarcassa). Germany: at VBL the full-time Vorstand members set the SAA at least annually, not the Verwaltungsrat.
November to mid-December
Fact
 Where a Q4 close is signed: ABP sets forward-year premium and indexation policy in November, VBL's Verwaltungsrat sat 14 November 2024 and ERAFP's Conseil d'administration met 16 December 2025.
www.vbl.de
 Final terms, closing mechanics and side-letter drafts.
April to May (France)
Fact
 FRR's Conseil de surveillance adopted the revised allocation strategique on 4 June 2026 and in June the prior year, and the Conseil meets at least twice a year, so anything for France must be in the June pack.
www.fondsdereserve.fr
 The France-facing case, landed April to May so it reaches the June board; missing June costs a year.
Mid-January to mid-March
Fact
 New-year budgets are live and Dutch executive boards are back to near-weekly cadence (ABP's uitvoerend bestuur met 40 times in 2024).
www.abp.nl
 A first-close-confirmed re-approach to anyone who slipped in Q4.
Mid-April to late May, and mid-September onward (insurers)
Fact
 Solvency II solo annual QRTs, the RSR and the SFCR are all due within 14 weeks of financial year end and quarterly QRTs within five weeks of quarter end, with group deadlines extended by six weeks under Article 312 - approach insurers only after those walls clear.
www.eiopa.europa.eu
 An Article 171a long-term-equity qualification argument alongside the fund materials, since the Type 2 equity charge is 49% plus the symmetric adjustment and falls to 22% only if the LTEI conditions are met.
Middle East sovereign and government investors
The year
A two-season year: a dense October to May working period cut in the middle by Ramadan and Eid (8 February to about 10 March 2027), bracketed by a near-total June to mid-September shutdown when heat and leadership travel empty the decision layer.
 October to early December
Fact
 Peak circuit density and the pre-Ramadan first-meeting runway: SuperReturn Middle East Dubai 13-15 October 2026, FII Riyadh 26-29 October 2026, Abu Dhabi Finance Week 7-10 December 2026.
fii-institute.org
 Full PPM and DDQ, with trips anchored to those three events. 1 June to mid-September (Dubai WMO 1991-2020 mean daily maxima are 40.0C in June, 41.5C July, 41.9C August, 39.5C September), plus the Ramadan and Eid block and the late-December lull; 2028 dates are 1 Ramadan on 28 January, Eid al-Fitr 26 February and Eid al-Adha 5 May, per the Umm al-Qura tabulation.
Decides: ADIA: the Private Equities department recommends to an Investment Committee chaired by the Managing Director, with the Board setting strategy and risk-return parameters. QIA: business decisions rest with the QIA Board and executive management, with the Supreme Council for Economic Affairs approving objectives, strategy and budget.
Mid-December to early February
Inference
 The calendar-year budget and allocation reset for the 31 December houses (ADIA, ADQ, Mubadala, Mumtalakat), plus Davos 18-22 January 2027.
www.adia.ae
 A revised allocation ask with a co-investment sweetener and side-letter drafts.
8 February to about 13 March 2027
Fact
 Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr - relationship only; Saudi Labor Law Article 98 caps Muslim working hours at six a day during Ramadan.
www.hrsd.gov.sa
 Iftar and majlis attendance; no IC-forcing asks and no data-room deadlines.
Mid-March to end of May
Fact
 The strongest window of the cycle: Saudi Capital Market Forum 22-24 March 2027, AIM Congress Dubai 12-14 April 2027, Qatar Economic Forum 27-29 April 2027, Milken Global 2-5 May 2027 - with Eid al-Adha around 16-17 May plus Hajj removing about two weeks.
milkeninstitute.org
 Closing documents, final IC packs, LPA negotiation and the signature push.
Mid-September to December
Fact
 Re-entry after the summer; ADIA's annual Review lands in this stretch (the 2025 Review was published 10 September 2026).
www.adia.ae
 Second-close and re-up conversations.
APAC-domiciled institutions (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Australia)
The year
Staggered fiscal years: Japan closes 31 March with plans landing April to May, Korea and Taiwan run calendar years (Korea's allocation resolved end-May, Taiwan tenders launch February to March), and Australia closes 30 June with APRA's performance test published by 31 August - so Q4 2026 is served by an October to November Korea and Australia push with Japan re-approached in the January to March budget window.
 January to March, and April to June (Japan)
Fact
 GPIF's alternatives Manager Registration is open continuously with no deadline (evaluation starts 1 June and continues at any time thereafter); Japan Post and the life insurers announce fiscal-year results and next-year strategy in May.
www.gpif.go.jp
 A GPIF registration entry plus DDQ, and Q1 introductions to the lifers ahead of the April plan. Late December to early January in Australia, the 25 March to 10 April Japanese fiscal close plus Golden Week, Korean Chuseok and Lunar New Year, Taiwan's Lunar New Year, and July to August in Australia during year-end reporting and the performance test.
Decides: GPIF: the Board of Governors sets the Medium-Term Plan, alternatives are capped at 5% of total assets, and managers must be FIEA-registered or apply with a registered Gatekeeper. NPS: the Fund Management Committee sets asset allocation and targets, with individual GP commitments at the internal investment committee. BLF: sealed-bid tender scored by an evaluation panel. Taiwanese insurers: board-approved foreign-investment procedures under FSC rules capping privately offered funds at 2% of the insurer's funds (3% for qualifying insurers).
March to June (Korea)
Fact
 The NPS Fund Management Committee deliberates the five-year mid-term asset allocation and resolves target weights by end-May, and Korea Post and KTCU RFPs cluster March to June with two to six week windows.
fund.nps.or.kr
 Board registration and a direct introduction to NPS overseas alternatives before the May committee, plus responses to Korea Post RFPs as posted.
August to October (Korea second wave)
Fact
 A second RFP wave (Korea Post Savings offshore infrastructure equity due 7 September 2026, Korea Post domestic blind PE with a rookie-league tier) and KIC preparing its first mandates to Korean PE houses with selection around November; the new NPS CIO Lee Kyu-hong took office 14 September 2026.
www.kedglobal.com
 A direct fund-of-funds pitch to KIC and Korea Post Savings, plus an introduction to the new NPS CIO.
Mid-February to mid-March (Taiwan)
Fact
 The Bureau of Labor Funds' annual overseas mandate tenders: 2026 was announced 11 March, due 9 April and awarded 26 June (USD 1.6bn across four managers for five years), with a second round in July.
www.blf.gov.tw
 Nothing for Fund I - BLF requires global AUM of at least USD 5bn, three years' operating history and a presence inside Taiwan, and every verified tender is a public-markets mandate; target Cathay Life and Fubon Life directly instead.
September to November (Australia)
Inference
 Post-30 June year end and post-performance-test air; APRA publishes results by 31 August and the 2026 results came 28 August (547 products, 12 failures).
www.apra.gov.au
 A direct approach to the private-markets teams with a parallel briefing to the asset consultants (JANA, Frontier, Mercer).

What Jodi says on the call
  • The 83 small names are four jobs, not eighty relationships. Outsourced investment offices are used most in exactly this size band, so the entity worth covering is the gatekeeper.
  • A hundred-million-dollar foundation writing a one-million cheque cannot reach a billion-dollar fund directly. The route is a feeder or the consultant list, and Axiom cut its own US minimum to do exactly this.
  • On seasons, two of the assumptions in the market are wrong and each one costs a quarter. The big Canadian plans close on 31 March, not December. And in the United Kingdom, manager selection has moved from the councils to the pools by statute.
  • The one that changes the American plan work: at the large plans a fund commitment this size is a staff decision under delegated authority, not a board vote. Sell to staff and the consultant.
  • August is genuinely dead everywhere. July is not.
The slide changeNew slide 9, a twelve-month strip. Rows are the limited-partner classes, columns are the months, shaded where the window is open and greyed where it is shut. Mark the two dead zones in August and late December. One line under it: the fiscal year end that drives each row.

🎯Six more conversions, in the slide-6 format

Melissa asked“More slide-6 style conversion examples for L LPs.”
Six L institutions, each with the first move and who carries it.
Same five-step shape as slide 6, with three columns the current slide does not have: the concrete first move, the internal champion who carries the paper, and the objection that will come back. Every fit line is drawn from the institution’s own published holdings.

AP3 (Tredje AP-fonden) L

Stockholm · Holds one
Fit
Four Axiom Asia vintages on AP3’s own published schedule, at US$40m and US$50m a time, on a two to three year rhythm. The last one is 2021 and no successor appears in the June 2026 schedule.
First meeting
The Asia fund-of-funds slot, not the fund. Ask what AP3 wants the 2026 vintage of that line to do differently from the 2021 one.
Diligence
Geography mix against the incumbent, then the co-investment layer. AP3 publishes its holdings, so the comparison is already public and can be walked through in the meeting.
Investment committee
Board, on a published cadence of roughly seven meetings a year. Q1 2027 is the realistic slot.
Commitment
US$50m, which is AP3’s modal single-fund ticket across 149 commitments.
The first move
A one-page note to the head of alternative investments comparing Pavilion’s geography mix against the Axiom vintages AP3 already holds, sent against its own published schedule.
Internal champion
Head of alternative investments. AP3 runs a small team and the sponsor is the person who already owns the Axiom relationship.
Expected timeline
First meeting Q4 2026, investment committee Q1 2027, commitment H1 2027.
“"We already have Asia through Axiom."”
Answer. Correct, and the ask is the next vintage of that line rather than a replacement of it. The mix is different where it matters to you.

Ilmarinen L

Helsinki · Holds neither
Fit
A full stack of Asian flagship buyout funds already held at 31 December 2025, with single Asia positions above EUR 70m inside an EUR 8.8bn private equity book. Asia is bought one manager at a time and never through a diversified vehicle.
First meeting
Allocation capacity. Ilmarinen is preparing to raise its equity allocation by up to fifteen percentage points ahead of new Finnish pension rules.
Diligence
Whether a diversified vehicle adds anything to a book that already holds the large Asian names. The answer is mid-market access and co-investment flow, which single-manager flagships do not give.
Investment committee
In-house investment organisation under the chief investment officer. No external consultant gate.
Commitment
US$50m to US$80m, read off existing position sizes.
The first move
Reach the chief investment officer through the Finnish allocator circuit before the 2027 pacing round is written, with one page on mid-market access the flagships miss.
Internal champion
Chief investment officer. Finnish earnings-related insurers decide with small senior teams and few layers.
Expected timeline
First meeting Q4 2026, diligence Q1 2027, commitment mid 2027.
“"We buy Asia direct from the managers we know."”
Answer. You buy the large end direct. The part you do not reach is the mid-market and the co-investment beside it, which is the whole of this fund.

Teachers’ Retirement System of the State of Illinois L

Springfield, Illinois · Holds one
Fit
US$200m already committed across Asia Alternatives vehicles in the mid-2010s vintages, and continuous private-markets pacing since, with no Asia-dedicated fund named in the 2025 batches.
First meeting
The unrenewed Asia line. The plan kept pacing and the Asia slot stopped being filled.
Diligence
Consultant-gated. The private equity consultant screens before staff can recommend, and the screen is of the product rather than the underlying managers.
Investment committee
Board, with staff and the consultant doing the work in front of it. Commitments are approved in batches.
Commitment
US$50m to US$150m inside a multi-fund batch.
The first move
The consultant, not the plan. Get into the private equity consultant’s manager research process first, because a US public plan of this size will not diligence a first-time fund the consultant has not seen.
Internal champion
The private equity consultant, then the senior investment officer for private equity.
Expected timeline
Consultant contact Q4 2026, plan meeting H1 2027, board batch late 2027 or 2028.
“"We are not adding a first-time manager to a consultant-gated programme."”
Answer. Pavilion is a first-time fund, not a first-time investor. The record runs from 2012 on the balance sheet, and the Asia line here has been open since the mid-2010s.

Northern LGPS / Northern Private Equity Pool L

Manchester and Leeds · Holds neither
Fit
The three partner funds bought pan-Asia fund-of-funds in the 2007 to 2008 era, let all of them run to residual value and replaced none, while the pool kept writing US$60m to US$79m single-manager Asia cheques as recently as a 2025 vintage.
First meeting
A fifteen-year vacancy on the diversified Asia line, documented in the pool’s own published holdings schedule.
Diligence
Cost first. Local government pension pools are judged on fees, so the all-in load has to be presented net of the co-investment layer from the first page.
Investment committee
The joint committee, with the officer work done by the head of private markets at the largest partner fund. Manager selection sits with the pool, not the councils.
Commitment
US$60m to US$79m, the pool’s median ticket band.
The first move
The head of private markets at the partner fund that runs the pool’s private equity, with the pool’s own schedule showing the lapsed Asia fund-of-funds lines.
Internal champion
Officer, not member. The head of private markets carries the recommendation into the joint committee.
Expected timeline
Officer meeting Q4 2026, joint committee paper H1 2027, commitment in the 2027 series.
“"We have moved to direct single-manager funds in Asia."”
Answer. You have, at the large end. The lines you let lapse were the diversified ones, and nothing replaced them.

NZ Super Fund L

Auckland · Holds neither
Fit
The private equity target was lifted from three to five percent in April 2025, the buyout programme was relaunched with a lower-mid-market focus, and a buyout fund-of-funds manager was appointed in 2025. A programme being rebuilt, with a proven tolerance for the structure.
First meeting
The rebuild itself. A fund-of-funds appointment in 2025 says the structure is already approved here, which removes the argument that usually takes two meetings.
Diligence
In house and fast by institutional standards. The gate is the Asia case rather than the vehicle.
Investment committee
Internal, under the chief investment officer, with the board setting the target.
Commitment
Around US$50m, the bottom of the band rather than above it.
The first move
The director of private equity, while the head of private equity seat is being recruited and the programme is still being shaped.
Internal champion
Director of private equity. The programme owner is the buyer here, not the chief investment officer.
Expected timeline
First meeting Q4 2026, diligence Q1 2027, commitment H1 2027.
“"We just appointed a fund-of-funds manager."”
Answer. For buyout. The Asia sleeve is a separate decision and your existing Asia exposure is a 2007 mandate and a real assets ticket.

Cathay Life Insurance L

Taipei · Holds both
Fit
Three Asia Alternatives vintages on its own exchange filings, alongside a wide Asia single-manager book and anchor tickets in the hundreds of millions for secondaries.
First meeting
The regime change. New accounting and solvency rules both took effect on 1 January 2026, a new company president took office in May 2026 and the insurance private-equity rule was amended in September 2026. The whole alternatives frame is being re-set.
Diligence
Capital treatment before returns. An insurer prices the solvency charge first, so the conversation is about structure and look-through, not about Asia.
Investment committee
Group investment function at holding-company level, with the regulator in the background.
Commitment
US$30m to US$80m as a primary ticket, with a materially larger anchor or secondaries ticket available if the structure fits the capital rules.
The first move
Route through the holding company investment function with a structure note on the capital treatment, not a fund deck.
Internal champion
The group chief investment officer. No head of alternatives is named in any filing, so the entry point is the holdco seat.
Expected timeline
First meeting Q1 2027 after the regime settles, structure work through 2027, commitment late 2027.
“"We hold both Asia Alternatives and Axiom Asia already."”
Answer. Then this is not a third fund-of-funds commitment. It is the co-investment and secondaries sleeve beside them, which is where your ticket size actually is.
What Jodi says on the call

  • The three columns I added are the ones that decide whether a slide becomes a meeting: the first move, the person inside who carries the paper, and the objection that comes back.
  • Before these go on the slide, seven of the thirteen people named on the current slide 6 did not survive a source check. I would fix those in the same pass.

What could not be sourced

Listed rather than filled in. Nothing below appears as a claim anywhere on this page.

Lead time from first meeting to commitment - for every LP class in this calendar. No ILPA document, consultant white paper or plan investment policy publishes a figure. The only bounded, sourced clocks found anywhere are ERAFP's 17-month French public tender (March 2025 launch to 13 August 2026 award), Taiwan's BLF tender at about 3.5 months announcement to award, and Border to Coast's one-year Series commitment period. Every other 'X to Y months' in the market is folklore; do not put a number in the client deck.

Published manager-search or annual manager-research calendars for Callan, NEPC, Meketa, Verus/Cerity, Wilshire, Aksia, StepStone, Hamilton Lane, Cambridge Associates and Mercer. None publishes a cycle on its own site. The only documented cycle is what appears inside plan board materials (CalPERS with Meketa in June, Oregon with Aksia and Pathway in March, CalSTRS with Meketa semi-annually, LACERA with StepStone). This is itself a finding: there is no consultant search season to time against.

Texas TRS, New York State Common Retirement Fund and Florida SBA - all three sites bot-block (Imperva and Cloudflare 403). No board calendar, investment policy or delegation threshold verified for any of them, and Texas's 31 August fiscal year end could not be confirmed.

A general '30 June fiscal year end' rule for US public pensions is confirmed only for CalPERS and CalSTRS; treat the generalisation as inference.

Investment-committee meeting cadence, committee composition, and the CIO-versus-IC delegation split at US endowments and foundations. 'Quarterly' is established from published meeting calendars, not from any charter or survey. No primary source states it.

The asset threshold at which a foundation or endowment hires investment staff. Only inferable from the OCIO-usage curve (0% of endowments above USD 5bn outsource; NACUBO attributes this to having the resources and staffing internally).

Pensions & Investments' annual OCIO survey (403 to every fetch method), Cerulli's E&F-specific OCIO figures and Chestnut Advisory's global OCIO numbers - all paywalled or member-only.

CCSF 2025 private-equity-specific allocation percentages and any allocation split by size cohort - the 2025 release publishes alternatives as one bucket; the last PE-specific number is 2021.

A published PitchBook, Preqin or ILPA statistic on average LP commitment size by endowment AUM band. The USD 3.1-3.9m figure used here is derived from ADV Schedule D gross asset value per beneficial owner, not a published statistic.

Whether any OCIO has actually allocated small-client capital to Asia PE. ADV brochures disclose strategies, not manager rosters; establishing this would need Schedule D private-fund listings cross-referenced to client Form 990s.

iCapital per-fund minimums (no ADV Schedule D 7.B(1) under its CRD) and whether its USD 1.2tn figure is committed capital, market value or cumulative flow - undefined on its site. Also unknown whether CAIS still offers Asia access; the Asia Fund IV feeder's last Form D is dated 16 December 2019.

Global fund sizes for Axiom Asia and Asia Alternatives - Form D captures only the US Reg D slice, so every figure quoted here understates the funds.

Every *.moderngov.co.uk and most democracy.*.gov.uk hosts returned 403, so no LGPS pool joint-committee 2026 meeting dates were retrieved at all (Kent for ACCESS, Tameside for GMPF, Hampshire, Surrey, Carmarthenshire for WPP, Edinburgh, Derbyshire and 20-plus London boroughs). Only Cornwall and LPFA yielded dated 2026 calendars. Brunel, LGPS Central and LPPI render empty to a non-JS fetcher; Railpen and Nest are JS-only.

The exact month AP2 and AP4 formally vote the strategic asset allocation - both state it is annual and budget-linked, neither names the month. AP3's published annual wheel (June operating plan, December budget) is the closest proxy.

↑ Jump menu📩What I still need from you

Answers to the first two would change the shape of the outreach more than any further research on my side.

📊 1The Preqin or Dakota investor export for the other fund-of-funds

You sent the Axiom Asia investor export on 14 September and it produced 112 named LPs. The same export for HarbourVest Asia Pacific, Pantheon Asia, LGT Crown Asia-Pacific and Asia Alternatives would turn the public-record list in piece 2 into a complete one. Public filings catch US public pensions, UK LGPS funds and Australian super funds. They miss endowments, family offices, insurers and every Asian LP.

🤝 2Who you and the Pavilion team already know

The relationship column across all 353 institutions is empty because it is the one thing no public source holds. A name, a firm and how warm it is, even on 30 of them, reorders the whole call list.

📄 3The rest of the Pavilion materials

Six slides is the strategy. The review needs the track record by fund and vintage with net IRR, TVPI and DPI, the underlying GP list, the team page with tenure, and the fund terms document. Every serious LP asks for those four in the first meeting.

💳 4Whether US$50m is a floor or a preference

Several institutions on the Canada map size a single fund position below US$50m, and the eleven plans in Section B never write the cheque at all.

If Pavilion will take US$20m to US$25m, the addressable Canadian list widens and mid-size US and European names come back into range.

🇨🇳 5How the China-exclusion sleeve actually works

A side letter, a parallel vehicle or a separate close. Several of the institutions here have a written China policy, and the answer decides whether they can look at the fund at all.

🏗️ 6Whether Temasek is anchoring, and with how much

Every LP will ask inside the first ten minutes. A number with a source settles it. Silence reads as no.

🗑️ 7Pavilion's own coverage list and the do-not-contact names

Which institutions Pavilion has already approached, which are re-ups from earlier Pavilion funds, and who is off limits. Without it a share of this outreach duplicates the GP.

📞 8Two or three reference LPs who will take a call

Named existing Pavilion investors willing to speak to a prospect. In a first-time fund on a new brand this does more work than any slide.

🌎 9Which geographies are actually in your mandate

The work so far covers the US, Canada, the UK, the Nordics and continental Europe. Whether Australia, Japan, Korea, the Middle East and the Swiss and German family-office channel are yours or the GP's decides where the next sweep goes.

🗑 10Your CRM export

Column names and record IDs, so the next deliverable imports into your system instead of being retyped.

Sources are linked in every cell and in full in the CSV and workbook files.

The F: and I: notation is defined in the key above the first table of piece 2.

Where the record is silent the cell says not found rather than guessing.
